summary: > We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?" > > Asking that question also changed _when_ review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the...
content_html:
We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?"

Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague.

Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny.

— Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang, How the Claude Code team does code review

title: Fast post-quantum signature aggregation with lattice SNARKs
summary: Today we're releasing Aerie, which aggregates lattice-based signatures using lattice-based SNARKs
content_html:
Most major blockchains besides Bitcoin run on proof of stake, where validators vote on each block by signing it. Signature aggregation is what makes large validator sets practical. Ethereum uses BLS signatures, whose algebraic structure lets it combine tens of thousands of validator signatures every slot into a single group element. Solana, where validator votes have made up about three-quarters of all transactions, is adopting BLS aggregation too, as part of its Alpenglow upgrade.

But as useful as BLS is, it is not post-quantum — and in fact, no known post-quantum signature scheme aggregates this way. Post-quantum signatures are also 10 to 100 times larger than today’s elliptic-curve signatures, so without aggregation these signatures will bloat blocks — limiting throughput and raising the cost of running a node. This matters as blockchains carry a growing share of the world’s payments, from stablecoin transfers to payments made by AI agents.

SNARKs (Succinct Non-interactive Arguments of Knowledge) fix these issues: The “aggregate signature” becomes a single succinct proof that every signature in the batch verifies. The prevailing SNARK-based approach, central to Ethereum’s roadmap, pairs hash-based signatures with hash-based SNARKs. But this approach is slow because hash-based signatures are expensive to prove: A single laptop can’t keep up with a full slot of signatures, which is one reason Ethereum’s design splits the work across many provers and recursively merges their proofs.

That’s why today we’re releasing Aerie, which takes the opposite approach by aggregating lattice-based signatures using lattice-based SNARKs. Aerie supports Falcon, a lattice-based signature scheme that NIST has selected for standardization, in both its Falcon-512 and Falcon-1024 variants.

Aerie numbers at a glance

Aerie is fast enough that a single laptop can aggregate roughly an Ethereum slot’s worth of signatures on its own:

  • Fast to prove: On an Apple M4 Max laptop, without GPU acceleration, Aerie aggregates 32,768 Falcon-512 signatures in 0.65 seconds, or over 50,000 per second. For comparison, the Lean Consensus team’s 2026 plan targets 1,000 signatures per second.
  • Compact in size: About 42 bytes per signature, roughly 16x smaller than Falcon-512 signatures and about 30x smaller than Falcon-1024 signatures.
  • Fast to verify: Verifying the proof takes 54 milliseconds on one core, 10x faster than checking the signatures one by one.

A simpler design space

Aerie’s speed also makes a simpler aggregation design possible.

In Ethereum’s current plan, each proof from leanVM (the zkVM being developed as part of Lean Ethereum to aggregate hash-based signatures) covers only about 900 signatures. Covering a full slot therefore takes rounds of recursive merging, and each round can’t start until the previous round’s proofs arrive.

Recursion also adds risk: It is intricate and bug-prone, and each recursive step proves statements about the very hash function used to make the proofs non-interactive. So the security of the resulting proofs can’t be established even in the random oracle model.

With Aerie, a node that has collected a slot’s signatures produces one proof directly, with no intermediate proofs and no recursion. This approach:

  • leaves more time in each slot for collecting votes and propagating the block;
  • opens aggregation to more participants; and
  • simplifies recovery: If an aggregator fails, any node holding the same signatures can produce a replacement proof.

What makes Aerie fast?

Two things, both rooted in lattices.

The first is Akita (the lattice-based polynomial commitment scheme we built with LayerZero Labs), together with the sum-check-based proving techniques we developed on the road to Lattice Jolt. These techniques are highly parallel and well suited to GPUs, so Aerie has plenty of room to get even faster.

The second reason Aerie is fast is the relative lack of hashing in lattice signature verification. Hash-based signatures are verified by evaluating hundreds of hashes per signature. Aggregating them means proving all of those hash evaluations — and hashing is expensive to prove, typically adding over 100x overhead relative to computing the hash natively.

Lattice signatures are verified differently. The core checks are algebraic, and hashing plays only a small role: a handful of hash evaluations per signature, not hundreds.

Why Falcon signatures?

Falcon takes the lack of hashing especially far. It’s a hash-and-sign scheme whose hash takes only the message and a salt as input. So if the aggregate includes each signature’s salt, the verifier can compute every hash itself, and the proof needs to cover only the algebraic checks. That’s a big part of Aerie’s speed, and why we started with Falcon.

Falcon is also compact: Falcon-1024 reaches NIST’s highest security level with signatures about half the size of ML-DSA-44’s, the lowest-security ML-DSA parameter set.

We’re not suggesting every blockchain adopt Falcon. Its signing algorithm is complex, and it has historically been hard to fit on hardware wallets, relying on floating-point arithmetic and tens of kilobytes of working memory. Side-channel hardening is still an active area of work.

But these drawbacks are being addressed rapidly. Recent research has shown how to implement Falcon signing with fixed-point arithmetic instead of floating point, and NIST now plans to require this approach in the FN-DSA standard. A new implementation also cuts Falcon-512 signing to about 11 kB of RAM, small enough for the secure elements in hardware wallets. For both reasons, Falcon is far easier to deploy than it was even a year ago.

Hardware wallets are a challenge for stateless hash-based signatures too: The SPHINCS- variants light enough for a hardware wallet take from 47 seconds to over six minutes to sign on a Ledger secure element.

For chains that weigh Falcon’s trade-offs and choose it — as Solana is exploring and Algorand has deployed — Aerie offers a fast path to aggregation.

We’re also working on extensions that require proving some hashing: supporting ML-DSA, whose hash depends on the signature itself; and removing Falcon’s salts from the aggregate by proving its hash inside the SNARK. Recent advances like LaBinius offer paths to proving those few hashes efficiently. And we’re extending Aerie to hybrid signatures that pair a lattice signature with an elliptic-curve-based one, an important form of defense-in-depth. These extensions may not reach 50,000 signatures per second, but we still expect plenty of headroom over the 1,000 per second Ethereum has targeted.

The security case for lattices

There’s an active debate about lattice versus hash-based cryptography in blockchain design, sharpened by speculation about what AI might mean for cryptanalysis. We’ll make the full case for embracing lattices in a future post. The short version is this: No one can promise that new attacks won’t be found on lattices, or on any other cryptography. But speculative cryptanalytic risk must be weighed against the clear and present risks built into more complicated systems.

As noted above, Ethereum’s planned hash-only signature aggregation design relies on SNARK recursion, with the coordination overhead, bug surface, and unestablished security that come with that approach.

Hash-only designs also lean on non-standard constructions: Ethereum’s planned consensus and account signatures are custom schemes outside NIST’s standards, with the underlying hash still undecided. This limits support from hardware wallets for individual users, and from the hardware security modules and custody systems that institutions rely on.

Relying exclusively on hash-based cryptography may appear safer, but in designs like these, it can lead to more brittle systems. What matters is the security of the whole system. We believe a full embrace of lattice cryptography makes blockchains more secure and more functional, not less.

The privacy case for lattices

Private payments need encryption, not just signatures and proofs: Recipients must learn about the notes sent to them, viewing keys must grant read access, and encrypted mempools must hide transactions until they’re ordered.

Private payments matter to cypherpunks and financial institutions alike, and Ethereum already plans for them. The Ethereum Foundation’s strawmap, a draft long-term roadmap for its base layer, lists a private L1 with shielded transfers among its five “north stars,” alongside a hash-based post-quantum L1. Those two goals are in tension: Shielded transfers need encryption, and encryption is exactly what hashing alone cannot provide.

Those two goals are in tension: Shielded transfers need encryption, yet encryption is exactly what hashing alone cannot provide.

A classic result of Russell Impagliazzo and Steven Rudich shows that public-key encryption cannot be built from hash functions in a black-box way. The best hash-only alternative, Merkle puzzles, gives honest users only a quadratic advantage over attackers, and this is optimal: No protocol can do better when hashes are modeled as random oracles. Even advocates of hash-only designs acknowledge this.

So a private Ethereum, like any chain that supports private payments, will depend on structured cryptography somewhere in its stack — and in practice, that means lattices. ML-KEM, a lattice scheme, is NIST’s primary post-quantum encryption standard and is already deployed across much of the internet.

Are there workarounds? One proposed solution is to keep encrypted notes off-chain, so fewer ciphertexts sit in public forever. But this doesn’t avoid encryption: The notes must still reach their recipients encrypted, over messaging apps and other channels that are already moving to ML-KEM. And off-chain delivery has trade-offs of its own: a channel that must stay available, can observe metadata, and whose failure can leave recipients unable to find and spend their funds.

For post-quantum blockchains with privacy, then, avoiding lattices in signatures and proofs doesn’t actually remove the dependence on lattices; it just gives up the performance and simplicity lattices offer — the costs, without the benefits. So the real question isn’t whether to rely on lattices, but whether to forgo their benefits for a false sense of security.

More details on Aerie: proof size and performance

An Aerie proof is about 66 KiB, whether it covers 32,768 Falcon-512 signatures or 16,384 Falcon-1024 signatures. That’s on par with the most compact prior lattice-based approach: PSE’s benchmarks of LaBRADOR-based Falcon aggregation report about 74 KB for 10,000 signatures, though verification there takes seconds rather than milliseconds.

Because Aerie’s verifier computes each signature’s hash itself, it also needs each signature’s 40-byte salt. For large batches, the salts dominate: 32,768 of them take up about 1.3 MB, versus 66 KiB for the proof. Even so, the aggregate costs only about 42 bytes per signature, 16 times smaller than Falcon-512 signatures (666 bytes) and nearly 30 times smaller than Falcon-1024 signatures (1,280 bytes).

Some deployments avoid the salt cost entirely. Algorand’s deterministic Falcon makes signing deterministic, which lets it replace the random per-signature salt with a fixed value. Aggregating its signatures would need no salts at all, just the 66 KiB proof, with small changes to how Aerie handles the salt and signature encoding.

Measured against Falcon itself, Aerie’s prover is also cheap: On a single core, proving takes only about 8 times as long as standard Falcon verification of the same signatures, and 1.4 times as long as signing them.

 

Compared with Orthus, the fastest prior Falcon aggregation scheme, Aerie (on one core of the same AVX-512 server):

  • proves 1.5x faster,
  • verifies 38x faster, and
  • produces proofs 1.7x smaller.

Moreover, Aerie proves everything a standard Falcon verifier checks. Prior Falcon aggregation work did not: It left out the check that each signature is canonically encoded, so its aggregates could accept signatures that a standard Falcon verifier would reject.

We also compared Aerie with leanVM, which aggregates XMSS signatures, the stateful hash-based scheme Ethereum plans to use for consensus. On the same machine, Aerie aggregates 29x as many signatures per second (about 50,800 versus 1,770).

Stateful signatures like XMSS work well at the consensus layer, where each validator signs at most one message per slot, so the slot number itself can serve as the signing state. But they pose large risks at the execution layer: A user who signs from two devices, or restores a wallet from a backup, can reuse signing state and thereby let attackers forge signatures under their key. That’s why Ethereum plans a stateless hash-based scheme for account signatures. And stateless hash-based signatures are even costlier to aggregate: In leanVM’s latest published benchmarks, on the same laptop model, it aggregates them at about 820 per second, roughly 60x slower than Aerie. (The benchmarked configuration also caps each key at about 127,000 signatures; configurations that allow far more cost more at key generation but aggregate just as fast.)

***

The code is at a16z/aerie, and the paper is here.

Aerie is joint work by Alberto Centelles (Imperial College London), Quang Dao (Carnegie Mellon University), Justin Thaler (a16z crypto), and Mohammadtaghi Badakhshan (LayerZero Labs).

[Falcon](https://falcon-sign.info/) takes the lack of hashing especially far. It’s a hash-and-sign scheme whose hash takes only the message and a salt as input. So if the aggregate includes each signature’s salt, the verifier can compute every hash itself, and the proof needs to cover only the algebraic checks. That’s a big part of Aerie’s speed, and why we started with Falcon.

Falcon is also compact: Falcon-1024 reaches NIST’s highest security level with signatures about half the size of ML-DSA-44’s, the lowest-security ML-DSA parameter set.

We’re not suggesting every blockchain adopt Falcon. Its signing algorithm is complex, and it has historically been hard to fit on hardware wallets, relying on floating-point arithmetic and tens of kilobytes of working memory. [Side-channel hardening](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/2313) is still an active area of work.

But these drawbacks are being addressed rapidly. Recent research has shown how to implement Falcon signing with [fixed-point arithmetic](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1531) instead of floating point, and NIST [now plans](https://groups.google.com/a/list.nist.gov/g/pqc-forum/c/7z-y5qp-W2Y) to require this approach in the FN-DSA standard. A [new implementation](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/1915) also cuts Falcon-512 signing to about 11 kB of RAM, small enough for the secure elements in hardware wallets. For both reasons, Falcon is far easier to deploy than it was even a year ago.

Hardware wallets are a challenge for stateless hash-based signatures too: The [SPHINCS-](https://ethresear.ch/t/sphincs-minus-efficient-stateless-post-quantum-signature-verification-on-the-evm/25165) variants light enough for a hardware wallet take from 47 seconds to over six minutes to sign on a Ledger secure element.

For chains that weigh Falcon’s trade-offs and choose it — as [Solana is exploring](https://solana.com/news/quantum-readiness) and [Algorand has deployed](https://algorand.co/blog/technical-brief-quantum-resistant-transactions-on-algorand-with-falcon-signatures) — Aerie offers a fast path to aggregation.

We’re also working on extensions that require proving some hashing: supporting ML-DSA, whose hash depends on the signature itself; and removing Falcon’s salts from the aggregate by proving its hash inside the SNARK. Recent advances like [LaBinius](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/2103) offer paths to proving those few hashes efficiently. And we’re extending Aerie to hybrid signatures that pair a lattice signature with an elliptic-curve-based one, an important form of defense-in-depth. These extensions may not reach 50,000 signatures per second, but we still expect plenty of headroom over the 1,000 per second Ethereum [has targeted](https://hackmd.io/je_2gejPRPCm0ZBBUpP9lA#Post-Quantum-Cryptography-and-Aggregation).

## The security case for lattices

There’s an active debate about lattice versus hash-based cryptography in blockchain design, sharpened by speculation about [what AI might mean for cryptanalysis](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=k_CoOoDsZ5Y). We’ll make the full case for embracing lattices in a future post. The short version is this: No one can promise that new attacks won’t be found on lattices, or on any other cryptography. But speculative cryptanalytic risk must be weighed against the clear and present risks built into more complicated systems.

As noted above, Ethereum’s planned hash-only signature aggregation design relies on SNARK recursion, with the coordination overhead, bug surface, and unestablished security that come with that approach.

Hash-only designs also lean on non-standard constructions: Ethereum’s planned consensus and account signatures are custom schemes outside NIST’s standards, with the underlying hash still undecided. This limits support from hardware wallets for individual users, and from the hardware security modules and custody systems that institutions rely on.

Relying exclusively on hash-based cryptography may appear safer, but in designs like these, it can lead to more brittle systems. What matters is the security of the whole system. We believe a full embrace of lattice cryptography makes blockchains more secure and more functional, not less.

## The privacy case for lattices

Private payments need encryption, not just signatures and proofs: Recipients must learn about the notes sent to them, viewing keys must grant read access, and encrypted mempools must hide transactions until they’re ordered.

Private payments matter to cypherpunks and financial institutions alike, and Ethereum already plans for them. The Ethereum Foundation’s [strawmap](https://strawmap.org), a draft long-term roadmap for its base layer, lists a private L1 with shielded transfers among its five “north stars,” alongside a hash-based post-quantum L1. Those two goals are in tension: Shielded transfers need encryption, and encryption is exactly what hashing alone cannot provide.

Those two goals are in tension: Shielded transfers need encryption, yet encryption is exactly what hashing alone cannot provide.

A [classic result](https://doi.org/10.1145/73007.73012) of Russell Impagliazzo and Steven Rudich shows that public-key encryption cannot be built from hash functions in a black-box way. The best hash-only alternative, [Merkle puzzles](https://doi.org/10.1145/359460.359473), gives honest users only a quadratic advantage over attackers, and [this is optimal](https://eprint.iacr.org/2008/032): No protocol can do better when hashes are modeled as random oracles. Even advocates of hash-only designs [acknowledge](https://x.com/VitalikButerin/status/2107976296320106851) this.

So a private Ethereum, like any chain that supports private payments, will depend on structured cryptography somewhere in its stack — and in practice, that means lattices. ML-KEM, a lattice scheme, is NIST’s primary post-quantum encryption standard and is already [deployed across much of the internet](https://radar.cloudflare.com/adoption-and-usage#post-quantum-encryption-adoption).

Are there workarounds? One [proposed](https://x.com/VitalikButerin/status/2107976296320106851) solution is to keep encrypted notes off-chain, so fewer ciphertexts sit in public forever. But this doesn’t avoid encryption: The notes must still reach their recipients encrypted, over messaging apps and other channels that are already moving to ML-KEM. And off-chain delivery has trade-offs of its own: a channel that must stay available, can observe metadata, and whose failure can leave recipients unable to find and spend their funds.

For post-quantum blockchains with privacy, then, avoiding lattices in signatures and proofs doesn’t actually remove the dependence on lattices; it just gives up the performance and simplicity lattices offer — the costs, without the benefits. So the real question isn’t whether to rely on lattices, but whether to forgo their benefits for a false sense of security.

## More details on Aerie: proof size and performance

An Aerie **proof** is about 66 KiB, whether it covers 32,768 Falcon-512 signatures or 16,384 Falcon-1024 signatures. That’s on par with the most compact prior lattice-based approach: [PSE’s benchmarks](https://ethresear.ch/t/lattice-based-signature-aggregation/22282) of LaBRADOR-based Falcon aggregation report about 74 KB for 10,000 signatures, though verification there takes seconds rather than milliseconds.

Because Aerie’s verifier computes each signature’s hash itself, it also needs each signature’s 40-byte salt. For large batches, the salts dominate: 32,768 of them take up about 1.3 MB, versus 66 KiB for the proof. Even so, the aggregate costs only about 42 bytes per signature, 16 times smaller than Falcon-512 signatures (666 bytes) and nearly 30 times smaller than Falcon-1024 signatures (1,280 bytes).

Some deployments avoid the salt cost entirely. Algorand’s [deterministic Falcon](https://github.com/algorand/falcon) makes signing deterministic, which lets it replace the random per-signature salt with a fixed value. Aggregating its signatures would need no salts at all, just the 66 KiB proof, with small changes to how Aerie handles the salt and signature encoding.

Measured against Falcon itself, Aerie’s prover is also **cheap**: On a single core, proving takes only about 8 times as long as standard Falcon verification of the same signatures, and 1.4 times as long as signing them.

![](https://dwt2zme5yrom6.cloudfront.net/uploads/2026/10/aerie-performance_a16zcrypto-1024x689.png)

Compared with [Orthus](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/398), the fastest prior Falcon aggregation scheme, Aerie (on one core of the same AVX-512 server):

- proves 1.5x faster,
- verifies 38x faster, and
- produces proofs 1.7x smaller.

Moreover, Aerie proves everything a standard Falcon verifier checks. Prior Falcon [aggregation](https://eprint.iacr.org/2024/311) [work](https://ethresear.ch/t/lattice-based-signature-aggregation/22282) did not: It left out the check that each signature is canonically encoded, so its aggregates could accept signatures that a standard Falcon verifier would reject.

We also compared Aerie with [leanVM](https://github.com/leanEthereum/leanVM), which aggregates XMSS signatures, the stateful hash-based scheme Ethereum plans to use for consensus. On the same machine, Aerie aggregates 29x as many signatures per second (about 50,800 versus 1,770).

Stateful signatures like XMSS work well at the consensus layer, where each validator signs at most one message per slot, so the slot number itself can serve as the signing state. But they pose large risks at the execution layer: A user who signs from two devices, or restores a wallet from a backup, can reuse signing state and thereby let attackers forge signatures under their key. That’s why Ethereum plans a [stateless hash-based scheme](https://ethresear.ch/t/sphincs-minus-efficient-stateless-post-quantum-signature-verification-on-the-evm/25165) for account signatures. And stateless hash-based signatures are even costlier to aggregate: In leanVM’s [latest published benchmarks](https://github.com/leanEthereum/leanVM/blob/127510d14c98ade4e8a97646c44fa7f1ff5e752d/README.md#sphincs-aggregation), on the same laptop model, it aggregates them at about 820 per second, roughly 60x slower than Aerie. (The benchmarked configuration also caps each key at about 127,000 signatures; configurations that allow far more cost more at key generation but aggregate just as fast.)

\\*\\*\\*

The code is at [a16z/aerie](https://github.com/a16z/aerie), and the paper is [here](https://assets.layerzero.network/pdf/aerie.pdf).

summary: **[Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO](https://www.ft.com/content/11632d03-358c-454b-af95-d06d4072932b?syn-25a6b1a6=1)** The phrase "told investors" appears four times in this FT article, which reports on Anthropic's day of hosting ...
content_html:
Anthropic tells investors quarterly revenue up nearly 50% to $16.8bn ahead of IPO

The phrase "told investors" appears four times in this FT article, which reports on Anthropic's day of hosting investors on Wednesday. Lots of details in here from "people with knowledge of the matter".

Key things I learned from the article:

  • Q1 revenue (Jan/Feb/Mar) was "about $4.8bn"
  • Q2 (Apr/May/Jun) was $11.5bn
  • Q3 (Jul/Aug/Sep) was $16.8bn
  • In Q3: $1.70 in revenue for every $1 spent on "computing power"
  • Adjusted operating margins (excluding stock-based compensation) were 11%

This point about distillation is worth quoting in full (highlight mine):

The start-up has also clamped down on “distillation” — a controversial practice whereby rival AI labs train their models on the outputs of more advanced ones.

When rival companies “distil” their models from Anthropic’s models, that involves heavy usage and spending.

Anthropic told investors on Wednesday distillation accounted for 5 per cent to 7 per cent of revenue and that they had cut it back “materially” in the third quarter of the year, said four people with direct knowledge of the matter.

Napkin maths says that if distillation was 5% of their Q2 revenue (before they cut it back in Q3) then unnamed "other labs" spent over half a billion dollars distilling Anthropic's models in that quarter!

Also notable: Anthropic appear to no longer be leaning on "annualized run-rate revenue" (previously) in these communications to their investors.

content_html:
Tool: LaTeX renderer

Inspired by Paul Ford and Aboard Foundary's new web app Tiny Little Office, which provides a suite of web app content editors (a Word Processor, Outliner, Presentation Builder, Spreadsheet, Calculator, Drawing Tool, Diagram Maker, Animator, Calendar, and Trip Planner).

Tiny Little Office's signature trick is to store all of the document data in the #fragment section of the URL, so every document created using it becomes a bookmarkable and shareable link.

It also has an llms.txt file telling agents how to construct URLs that will render as documents. Claude used that file to generate this link to a deck that explains how the URL format works:

Tiny Little Office inspired me to have Claude Code (Opus 5.5 Extra) build a similar tool that works with LaTeX. Here's the sequence of prompts I used:

I want a tool where you can link to it with a fragment hash #code-here and it treats that code as LaTeX and renders it really effectively. It should also support a prefix which means the latex is compressed with a custom compression dictionary optimized for latex. Use the best available latex render library from a CDN (consider WebAssembly too). If loaded without a fragment hash show an editor you can paste latex into and then toggle to a "rendered" view. That rendered view should be bookmarkable. The #fragment view should let you switch to edit source too.

Since it was working in my tools repo I told it to take inspiration from the <iframe sandbox="..."> mechanism used by my existing SVG in Markdown tool as protection against XSS risks:

Safe from XSS? We could run in an iframe sandbox like we do on the SVG markdown render project

I had it copy the Gist/URL loading feature from that tool as well:

We should have an option to load latex from a URL (or gist) similar to the markdown SVG tool

Here's an example link. The tool uses Pako 2.1.0, MathJax 4.1.3, faster-latex 0.3.1, and DOMPurify 3.4.16.

content_html:
AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary.

Indie game developer Popcar talks about the recent wave of AI-powered decompilation of existing games, enabling weird mashups between existing games, and producing a boom in game preservation projects to get old games working on new hardware (often in a browser using WebAssembly).

I like how this piece captures both the positives and the negatives of this new development:

Most people already realized the scary part by now. If AI can decompile games and software, then the entire tech industry is about to explode. Anybody can decompile other software and use it any way they'd like, and nobody can stop them. Companies can steal from competitors. Your paid game or app can be open-sourced against your will. This isn't exclusive to old video games, we can apply this to any software. [...]

This is also a big win for preservation. Old games can be ported, modified, enhanced, and made much more easily accessible than before. [...[

With console makers going all in on digital and games becoming entirely unplayable due to servers shutting down, this is fantastic news. We could own software we bought regardless of what the company thinks.

Via Hacker News

content_html:
Redesigning source control at Anthropic

Interesting piece from Anthropic describing why and how they built their own custom alternative to Git, based on the dramatic increase in rate of changes to their code after the past six months.

In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day.

They included a chart showing those changes. I had Claude modify their chart (code here) to add markers for the public releases of each of their models in 2026:

This shows public release dates, not the date when models became available for Anthropic's internal use. My guess is that the introduction of Fable/Mythos class models is a key factor in the increased coding velocity.

"Antique" is their new code review system. The source control system is called Scion, and sounds to me like a reinvention of centralized source control along the lines of Subversion.

(Update: Anthropic credit Google's Piper and Meta's Sapling as "prior art" - it looks like the core concept of "derived data" was heavily inspired by Mononoke, the server component of Sapling.)

They had some pretty extreme requirements:

The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day.

The new system was built by a team of seven people, and the migration from Git was completed in five months.

When asked on Hacker News about the lack of offline support, Scion engineer Nick G replied:

Since Claude is by far the heaviest user of Scion and is necessarily online, this just wasn't important to do.

As an aside, I've been trying adversarial review in my own projects recently, where you have a model try and find flaws (I often play Claude and GPT off against each other). This note from the article reflected my own experience with that:

Anthropic also makes extensive use of adversarial review, and, while this is incredibly effective in many ways, it can also be myopic, so skilled engineers needed to steer Claude away from over-engineering parts of the system in response to hypothetical concerns.

Via Hacker News

Release: llm-gemini 0.35

I added support to llm-gemini for the new Gemini 4 Argon model, made available today via the Gemini API and for customers of their $100/month subscription plan.

Here are the low, medium and high pelicans. As expected, they are all excellent: Gemini has a track record of producing great SVGs, and are the only lab where I know their staff have invested in SVG specifically (and who have boasted about their pelicans before.)

Here's the "high" illustration, which cost me 17.166 cents:

The pricing is interesting. At launch, Argon is $2/million input and $10/million output - the same price as GPT-6 Sol, half the price of Claude Opus 5.5 and 1/5th the price of Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra.

But on December 1st Argon is set to double in price - so it will be the same price as Opus 5.5.

Prices like this aren't really comparable these days since what really matters is how many tokens a model takes to achieve a goal within an agentic harness.

One useful clue for that comes from Artificial Analysis, who publish the total cost to run their benchmark using each model. Argon is looking very good there - costing $2,407 to run the benchmark, putting it close to GLM-5.3 and significantly cheaper than OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta's latest models.

When the price doubles it will still be a little cheaper than GPT-6 Astra.

(I used ChatGPT to edit that chart! The data is all correct, I checked - I needed to get that Gemini 4 Argon info box to display without overlapping the other numbers.)

Some bonus examples using Gemini 4 Argon: here's Generate an SVG of an armadillo in fishnet tights jaywalking on Mars, here's a Fabergé egg it created for me using Blender, and DeepMind staffer @fofrAI shared a video of a pelican riding a bike, using fourier epicycles. That's a fun new twist!

title: How Far Crypto Has Come in Washington
summary: Clarity hasn’t passed, but the critics miss how far crypto policy has come in three years.
content_html:
I’ve been reading the postmortems on Clarity, and some of the criticism is fair. Clarity is the industry’s biggest legislative priority. We worked hard on it. And it hasn’t passed the Senate. That’s a setback, and it deserves serious accounting. But much of the commentary describes an industry that made a huge effort in Washington and came away empty-handed.

You have to leave out a lot of the story to tell it that way.

Less than three years ago, a founder building a crypto company in America faced a basic question: am I going to be allowed to do this?

And it was a reasonable question. The SEC was suing major companies across the industry, there was no workable framework for ensuring these projects could comply with the law, and the official position was that everyone already had all the rules they needed. Builders had few options. They could hire more lawyers, leave the United States, or both.

The industry had already been through the fight over sweeping crypto tax-reporting provisions in the 2021 infrastructure bill. Then FTX turned out to be a spectacular fraud, and people who had nothing to do with it spent the next year explaining that blockchain technology had nothing to do with it. Founders headed overseas. Trying to persuade Washington to work on crypto regulation in that environment went about as well as you’d expect.

The goal has always been simple: establish clear rules so people can build here and customers are protected.

The industry has been working toward that goal for the better part of a decade. For much of that time, simply getting taken seriously in Washington was a project. So the community built the capacity to do something about it: policy teams, political operations, coalitions. Founders came to Washington to explain the fundamentals of blockchain networks to people who mostly knew crypto from its worst headlines.

There was nothing inevitable about what followed. And yet that work produced significant results.

Start with stablecoins. The U.S. now has a federal law governing their issuance, with requirements for the companies behind them and protections for customers. GENIUS is law, other countries are following suit, and agencies are working through implementation. We’ve gone from debating whether Washington would ever pass meaningful crypto legislation to working through how a major crypto law gets implemented.

That’s just the most visible achievement. Last year, Congress also overturned the IRS’s DeFi broker rule, a data collection mandate that was essentially impossible for blockchain software to comply with. The SEC also rescinded SAB 121, removing a major accounting obstacle to institutions holding crypto for customers, and FinCEN just withdrew the dangerous “Unhosted Wallet Rule”. These were threats and barriers that companies were spending time and money figuring out how to live with. They’re now gone.

Then there’s the proactive work happening at the agencies. The SEC has proposed a framework for raising money through token offerings and new rules for safeguarding crypto assets. It has issued an exemption allowing certain tokenized stocks to trade onchain. The CFTC just proposed a path for regulating centralized exchanges. And the SEC and CFTC have provided guidance on how existing law applies to crypto assets, helping to answer questions of critical importance to the industry, such as: How do you launch a token? How can it trade? Who can hold assets for customers, and what obligations should they have?

These are some of the very questions the industry spent years trying to get Washington to answer. They’re also central to the effort behind Clarity.

The House has now passed comprehensive crypto market structure legislation twice, with bipartisan support: FIT21 in 2024 and Clarity in 2025. And a great deal of that work is moving forward through agency proposals, guidance, and exemptions, even though the bill isn’t law. The U.S. government is working out the conditions under which crypto projects can operate safely here, which was the point all along — and still is.

There is an obvious limitation here. Proposed rules aren’t final. Guidance and exemptions only go so far. A company making a ten-year investment would understandably like to know that the rules won’t depend on the outcome of every presidential election. That is a big part of why the industry pushed so hard for Clarity. Legislation can settle questions agencies can’t settle on their own and give companies a foundation that lasts beyond whoever happens to be in charge.

The job isn’t finished. Getting legislation signed into law is hard, even when there is broad agreement that it’s needed. We need rules that companies can count on for the long-term, whether through durable rulemaking or legislation. We’ll continue to push for Clarity and other laws that set clear rules and protect consumers.

Not long ago, founders were making plans around the possibility that they couldn’t stay in America. That’s not the case anymore. We have a federal stablecoin law and regulators are at work writing a raft of sensible rules for everyone to follow.

Now we need to make sure the progress lasts. That is a problem to solve. It is also a very different problem from the one we had three years ago.

If the agent isn't using my diagnostics library, I could introspect and update AGENTS.md, but there's still a delta, and it'll drift. Instead, I write a pre-commit hook that checks the git diff for direct calls to observability modules that bypass my diagnostics module. Boom: fail the commit, inject a prompt telling the agent to use the diagnostics library. All of a sudden it's ten out of ten.

— Geoffrey Huntley, nobody should type code by hand anymore. here's what's left.
