“Know Your Customer” (KYC) checks are often seen as an obstacle to bringing traditional finance onchain and to growing DeFi overall.

For anyone unfamiliar, these checks are a necessary part of financial institutions’ obligations under the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) to combat money laundering and terrorist financing.[1](#endnote-1) The process requires coordination among issuers, verifiers, and regulators with different incentives, timelines, and legal requirements.

For banks, broker-dealers, and other BSA-covered institutions bringing tokenized products onchain, the challenge is reaching more customers and accessing liquidity, while meeting compliance requirements that can add time and complexity. Onboarding a new customer, for example, often means repeating identity checks that were already completed somewhere else. Fortunately, new KYC tools designed specifically for blockchains may help make verification more reusable than methods we’ve inherited from traditional finance.

The starting point is understanding _who_ an institution needs to identify. In traditional finance, institutions transact through networks of identified intermediaries, and each institution satisfies its own KYC obligations. The same principle applies onchain in that the bank’s customer-identification obligations apply to its own customers and not to every participant in the underlying settlement infrastructure.

Customer identification rules focus on who opens an account with the bank. On that reading, someone does not become the bank’s customer simply by transacting with one of its customers or by trading against a liquidity pool the bank supplies.[2](#endnote-2) A bank can satisfy its BSA obligations through an appropriate compliance program covering its own customers and transactions, [regardless of which blockchain network or protocol settles them](https://a16zcrypto.com/posts/article/financial-integrity-framework-permissionless-networks).

The U.S. Department of the Treasury is currently thinking through how financial institutions can use these new technologies and methods to satisfy AML/CFT program requirements, including for CIP/KYC. Given the passage of the GENIUS Act, regulators are now tasked with understanding and pursuing innovative methods and standards for meeting these modern AML/CFT objectives more effectively.

Below we take a look at the legal and practical conditions for reusable KYC, then explore how tools like zero-knowledge proofs, verifiable credentials, nontransferable tokens, and blockchain analytics could help. Finally, we look ahead to “Know Your Agent”: identifying AI agents, whom they represent, and what they’re authorized to do.

## Adapting KYC for an onchain world

Traditional KYC happens institution by institution. Each verifies a customer’s identity at onboarding through its Customer Identification Program (CIP), keeps its own records, and conducts ongoing Customer Due Diligence (CDD). That record lives with the institution, which becomes a trusted intermediary. Customers have to repeat this process at each new institution, even when assets move between people and businesses whose identities have already been checked.

Blockchain transactions add another layer of complexity. Assets move across chains, protocols, and wallets, often without an intermediary performing KYC. A wallet might have originated from a BSA-obligated exchange, a DeFi protocol, or a consumer app. Each of these services has its own risk and liability frameworks, which may vary by jurisdiction. Some intermediaries have no KYC obligations at all. Even where KYC is required, there is no standardized regulatory framework to carry the result from one institution to the next. Institutions often repeat verification of the same user, adding cost and delays.

As former SEC Commissioner Peirce recently [noted](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/speeches-statements/peirce-looking-change-haystacks-remarks-sifma-s-digital-assets-conference-092326), “the approach to ferreting out illicit finance \[…\] has been the same: collect more and more data. The approach is not working particularly well, and technology has outpaced our legacy approach, so it is time for a change.”

Financial institutions, blockchain developers, and regulators are now creating new methods for meeting KYC and AML/CFT goals. One approach is letting institutions reuse identity checks completed by others. For that to work, institutions need clear rules about whose checks they can trust and who is responsible for compliance.

## Reusability and the ecosystem of trust

Users want to do KYC once and have it work everywhere, known interchangeably as _reusable KYC_, _reliance KYC_, [_federated_](https://dwt2zme5yrom6.cloudfront.net/uploads/2025/11/Comment-Letter-Treasury-re-Illicit-Finance.pdf) KYC, or _hosted KYC_.

Customers repeat verification offchain as well. Someone opening accounts at two banks will need to complete KYC at each, but most customers do not form these relationships often. In crypto, however, users often onboard to new products, and there’s no trusted intermediary to carry the KYC through the life of a transaction.

Institutions do not want to avoid KYC; they want to avoid _redundant_ KYC. Every time a user wants to interact with a new exchange or application, the KYC process starts from scratch, which is expensive for the platform, creates friction for the user, and is increasingly unreliable as deepfake tools proliferate. Banks and other BSA-covered entities have become burdened by identity verification methods that are costly, privacy-invasive, and ineffective at deterring illicit finance.

Institutions do not want to avoid KYC; they want to avoid redundant KYC.

Repeated verification can mean sharing sensitive personal information with more institutions. Even when presented digitally, a government ID can compromise a customer’s safety and increase the risk of targeted fraud, stalking, identity theft, and other unauthorized uses of that information. A mobile ID typically discloses a customer’s full legal name, residential address, date of birth, and photograph, all in one disclosure.

These “honeypots” of sensitive personally identifiable information (or PII) are tempting to financial criminal actors, and the stakes are high if any of this information is intercepted, mishandled, or held onto longer than necessary by the bank. As Coin Center has [pointed out](https://coincenter.org/tear-down-this-walled-garden/), the current system forces individuals to “repeatedly surrender their sensitive personal information to centralized databases at tremendous personal risk.” To avoid these unwarranted vulnerabilities, privacy advocates have urged regulators to consider alternative ways to digitally verify a customer’s identity beyond simply government-issued identification records.

A useful analog in traditional financial markets is SWIFT’s KYC Registry (although the name is something of a misnomer; it focuses on bank-to-bank relationships and is more accurately a KYB registry). Banks already use SWIFT, a global messaging network, to communicate cross-border payment instructions. And when SWIFT launched its KYC Registry in 2014, it extended that infrastructure to compliance: Banks upload their documentation once and share it with any counterparty that needs it. The registry now spans nearly 8,000 institutions across 200+ countries and works because the relationships are institution-to-institution and the counterparties are known.

Crypto has no equivalent centralized registry. If Coinbase has already verified a user to bank-grade standards, can that verification be inherited? If Robinhood’s KYC’ed users want to access an onchain credit protocol, can the compliance work that Robinhood already did travel with them?

This is known as “whitelisted liquidity.” Access to pools of pre-verified users is, in practice, a form of compliance distribution, but is not a legal requirement. An institution’s own obligations are the same whether its customers trade in a gated pool or a permissionless one. And for tokenized securities, gating a pool and setting standards for who may trade in it can itself carry regulatory obligations under the SEC’s recent innovation exemption. Issuers are already seeking introductions to global exchanges specifically to leverage their compliance frameworks, but the commercial structure is still being developed.

### Outsourcing versus reliance

New solutions tailored to crypto can minimize harmful data collection and produce auditable, verifiable alternatives to the same old “box-checking” KYC. In fact, there are a growing number of examples of reliance KYC being used in the crypto space.

KYC reliance can also be described as an “ecosystem of trust,” where a larger KYC provider (or group of providers) with enough scale creates their own trust network, similar to the concept of “single sign-on.” Examples include providers such as Sumsub ID, World ID, MoonPay, and Stripe through Privy. Basic verification might run from $1 to $2 per initial verification charged to the originating platform, and then any secondary platforms only have to go through a partial KYC process (such as a liveness check), which reduces their cost per customer.

One recent example is the Fireblocks Open Transaction Layer (OTL), which is an open protocol stack that standardizes identity, compliance, and messaging across participants in onchain finance. Notably, KYC is done by existing regulated entities in the network, not by OTL itself. OTL creates a shared protocol so when one of those institutions has verified a user, that status can be recognized by other participants without re-verification.

A similar concept is Privado ID (formerly Polygon ID, which spun out from Polygon Labs in 2024 and recently merged with Disco.xyz), which makes existing KYC [portable](https://www.privado.id/blog/reusable-ekyc---the-fintech-white-whale). Issuers, including government institutions, banks, and KYC providers, generate verifiable credentials. The user requests, collects, and stores this credential in their identity wallet. Verifiers can then query the user’s wallet for the appropriate credentials, whether offchain or [onchain](https://docs.privado.id/docs/verifier/on-chain-verification/overview).

SpruceID offers another solution built around identity standards. Trusted sources, such as the DMV or a state licensing agency, issue verifiable digital credentials that users store on their phones. These tools make it easier to reuse verified information, but institutions still need to understand their legal responsibilities when using another provider’s work.

Institutions can use outside providers for KYC, but the legal treatment depends on the provider and the arrangement. Under the [BSA’s customer-identification rules](https://bsaaml.ffiec.gov/manual/AssessingComplianceWithBSARegulatoryRequirements/01), “reliance” is a specific legal provision that applies only when relying on another _regulated financial institution_. Using a provider that does not qualify, such as an identity-verification vendor or credit bureau, is treated as outsourcing. In that case, the institution remains responsible for meeting its CIP requirements.

![Table comparing legal reliance on federally regulated financial institutions with outsourcing to third-party vendors under the BSA: section, ultimate liability, and requirements](https://dwt2zme5yrom6.cloudfront.net/uploads/2026/10/KYA-frameworks-table-selection-scaled.png)

Similarly, the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), the international body that sets AML/CFT standards, [recommends](https://www.fatf-gafi.org/content/dam/fatf-gafi/recommendations/FATF%20Recommendations%202012.pdf.coredownload.inline.pdf) that countries may permit financial institutions to rely on third parties for certain customer due diligence measures if three conditions are met:

1. The third party is itself subject to AML/KYC regulation and supervision and has those compliance measures in place;
2. The relying institution has immediate access to the underlying KYC data on request; and
3. The relying institution retains ultimate legal liability for the compliance outcome.

This doesn’t always neatly map to crypto. First, the “immediate access” requirement means the underlying PII has to be producible on demand to a regulator or law enforcement. This is in direct tension with the privacy-preserving design of most onchain KYC solutions.

Separately, many crypto platforms are not “regulated institutions” for purposes of the federal AML/CIP reliance rule, even where they are registered money services businesses or state-chartered trust companies with their own AML obligations. This means they can’t be counterparties in a formal reliance relationship (although this is evolving as more crypto firms become licensed).

This is one of the hurdles Treasury will have to resolve when considering more flexible, crypto-native CIP methods. Decentralized methods may be more cost-effective and efficient, and may better protect user privacy and guard against cybersecurity breaches, but law enforcement will still need to have a trusted source, somewhere, for the truth (i.e., who the customer is and what entity can produce documentary evidence to further an investigation or prove attribution in court).

In addition to AML program requirements, financial institutions also have to consider their obligations under the Funds Transfer Rule, widely referred to as the “Travel Rule.” Any financial institution or virtual asset service provider (VASP), which in the U.S. would include BSA-covered institutions that transfer funds above a certain threshold (typically $3,000, although other jurisdictions set a lower threshold amount), must collect and transmit identifying information about both the sender and the recipient to the next institution in the chain. In traditional finance this is straightforward because banks already hold KYC data and have established messaging rails such as SWIFT to pass it through. In crypto, the blockchain transaction and the KYC information travel separately.

Many established providers offer crypto-specific Travel Rule compliance solutions. Examples include the industry-led Travel Rule Universal Solution Technology (TRUST), originally launched by an industry coalition including Coinbase, and similar products from Notabene and Sumsub.

In the U.S., Travel Rule messaging is only required between financial institutions. Financial institutions and VASPs are not expected to send this data to parties that are neither financial institutions nor VASPs, such as self-hosted wallets.

Financial institutions should not lose sleep over Travel Rule compliance when interacting with non-intermediary blockchain technology such as DeFi and self-hosted wallets. A bank or crypto exchange may still ask customers for this information for transactions to and from self-hosted wallets or outside of BSA-covered institutions. It may do so as part of its own risk-based AML/CFT program, but the Travel Rule does not require this.

Financial institutions should not lose sleep over Travel Rule compliance when interacting with non-intermediary blockchain technology such as DeFi and self-hosted wallets.

That said, non-U.S. jurisdictions have considered and may take a different position with respect to threshold amounts for triggering the rule and whether VASPs must collect data from non-VASP entities or persons. Jurisdictions are still working out how to apply KYC, AML, and Travel Rule requirements onchain.

The good news is that new, affirmative legislation is unnecessary in the U.S. Existing laws and frameworks can be adapted through interpretive guidance, rulemaking, or innovation exemptions. Congress has already endorsed the basic allocation of responsibility described above. The GENIUS Act places AML and sanctions obligations on the permitted stablecoin issuer, the identifiable entity at the application layer, and not on the permissionless networks its stablecoins circulate on. Regulators have also recognized the role new technologies can play in compliance. In its April 2026 proposal, FinCEN [identified](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-04-10/pdf/2026-07033.pdf) “machine learning, generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), digital identity, blockchain monitoring and analytics, or application programming interfaces (APIs)” as relevant innovative approaches to meeting regulatory obligations.

New, affirmative legislation is unnecessary in the U.S. Existing laws and frameworks can be adapted through interpretive guidance, rulemaking, or innovation exemptions.

In the same proposal, FinCEN [expressed](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2026-04-10/pdf/2026-07033.pdf) support for financial institutions’ adoption of emerging tech, stating that institutions that “responsibly experiment with innovative technologies in their AML/CFT programs will not incur any additional risk of being subject to a significant supervisory AML/CFT action or AML/CFT enforcement action solely based on the use of innovative technologies.”[3](#endnote-3) To give institutions more certainty about how this applies in practice, the crypto industry [has urged](https://dwt2zme5yrom6.cloudfront.net/uploads/2026/06/Andreessen-Horowitz-a16z-response-to-FinCEN-and-OFAC-06.09.2026.pdf) FinCEN and supervisory banking agencies to concretely confirm through rules or written guidance when forms of digital identity can be used to meet AML program requirements, including for CIP/KYC.

Even with clearer guidance, not every KYC determination can be reduced to a binary cryptographic proof. Such proofs may help confirm a birth date, citizenship, the result of a sanctions check, or possession of a credential. But more complex, judgment-intensive AML inquiries may still require traditional diligence.

Verifiable credentials could support or replace particular components of CIP/KYC rather than eliminate risk-based customer due diligence altogether. Treasury’s current rules already allow non-documentary verification methods and leave the mix of methods to the bank’s risk-based judgment. [The September 2026 interagency FAQs](https://www.fincen.gov/system/files/2026-09/MDL-VDC-FAQs.pdf) expressly recognize that qualifying verifiable digital credentials can be used within a bank’s CIP, though they do not approve every decentralized identifier or credential design.

FinCEN and the relevant banking agencies could build on this guidance under existing authority. Options include interpretive guidance or additional FAQs, targeted exemptions, pilot programs followed by regulatory approval, standards for credential issuers, or amended regulations. These approaches could allow traditional financial institutions and other qualified public or private entities to issue verified credentials under common standards, reducing the need for each bank to independently reconstruct the same identity file.

Until then, financial institutions can already adopt tools that meet current requirements. The following approaches show how this could work.

## The solutions

Institutions could benefit from a trusted, compliant backend that makes identity reusable across onchain applications. A trusted provider could verify a customer’s identity and issue a digitally signed credential recording the result. The customer could then present that credential to other applications, which could check who issued it and whether it meets their own verification requirements.

This isn’t a new concept. It goes back at least to the idea of the [soulbound token](https://vitalik.eth.limo/general/2022/01/26/soulbound.html) Vitalik Buterin outlined in 2022, where a nontransferable token is issued to a person’s wallet. Related work includes W3C’s work on decentralized identifiers (DIDs) and verifiable credentials (VCs), which is not specific to crypto.

In practice, a trusted issuer, such as an “approved” or regulated KYC provider, a bank, or potentially a government, could verify a user’s identity and issue a credential. That credential could be stored in the user’s wallet and selectively disclosed to any application that requires it.

Likewise, [zero-knowledge proofs](https://a16zcrypto.com/posts/tags/zero-knowledge-succinct-proof-systems) allow users to prove they are KYC’ed without revealing their PII, adding privacy to this process. With these, users could reuse the credential where it meets the receiving institution’s CIP requirements, potentially reducing repeated checks.

Verification also needs to be composable, meaning applications can incorporate it into their own compliance checks. More specifically, to be most effective, issuers and platforms should be able to embed that logic in the token contracts and application-level smart contracts they control. This would allow them to apply their compliance requirements without bolting them on or pushing them down into the base layer network.

## Approaches

Other viable tools for satisfying the necessary aspects of financial institutions’ risk-based AML program requirements are “Know Your Wallet” (KYW), “Know Your Asset” (KYA), and “Know Your Transaction” (KYT). These methods are already used by many exchanges and money transmitters as part of their overall AML program.

### Know Your Wallet

Know Your Wallet connects identity checks to the blockchain address a customer uses, helping institutions establish who controls it and which assets or services that customer is eligible to access. KYW can combine:

- **Identity binding**, linking a real-world identity to a wallet address, usually through a KYC check at onboarding;
- **Liveness and uniqueness**, confirming the identity is real, human, and not duplicated across wallets, including a periodic refresh of the linkage to ensure that this is the same real-world identity linked to the same wallet address; and
- **Eligibility/permissions**, meaning a wallet, once confirmed, has specific permissions (Is it accredited/qualified? Is it in a permissible jurisdiction? Is it flagged to hold certain asset types?). This is the compliance eligibility layer.

Crypto KYC largely follows the traditional playbook. Companies like Onfido, Veriff, Trulioo, Socure, Incode, ID.me, Persona, Sumsub, and Sardine offer identity binding and document verification, liveness detection, and AML screening. These identity checks generally take place offchain and do not, by themselves, establish which blockchain address a person controls. Linking the verified identity to an address is an additional step (although Sumsub has started to expand into wallet-based KYC by allowing users to link their wallet addresses).

Onchain applications can use nontransferable tokens to record verification results, zero-knowledge proofs to limit disclosure of personal information, and proof-of-personhood systems to help verify that each user is a unique human. These approaches can work together.

The approach uses nontransferable, non-sellable tokens, often called soulbound tokens, which are permanently attached to a specific wallet address. In a KYW system, a provider could verify a user’s identity offchain and then issue a token to their wallet as a record of that verification. One solution, Quadrata, generates a soulbound token to check for attributes like country and age.

These tokens can make it easier to verify audit records, but nontransferability alone does not prevent another person from taking control of the wallet. For instance, if someone’s wallet is transferred, the token may no longer identify the person controlling it. Systems also need mechanisms for credential expiration and revocation. Those capabilities depend on the implementation; Quadrata, for example, supports issuer-controlled revocation.

A related approach embeds compliance conditions in asset tokens. DTCC’s [ComposerX](https://www.dtcc.com/digital-assets/composerx), a tokenization platform for financial institutions, uses the Compliance Aware Token Framework (CATF) to enforce regulatory and transaction rules as transactions execute. This allows asset transfers to depend on compliance conditions being met.

Other startups, such as Burrata, aimed to issue identity tokens as well, and while this was technically viable, they were “ [unable to find](https://www.burrata.xyz/) product market fit” and shut down.

Zero-knowledge proofs address another facet of the problem, allowing a user to prove a claim about their identity without revealing the underlying data. There are a number of solutions that issue a ZK proof from an ID scan.

- Self.xyz offers privacy-preserving “pre-KYC,” where users scan their physical passport and generate a zero-knowledge proof of the passport data, proving attributes such as someone being over 18 and not on a sanctions list. It is useful as a gating layer before formal KYC, saving time by screening out bots or sanctioned wallets.
- Aztec, a privacy-focused Layer-2 blockchain on Ethereum, acquired zkPassport, which has a similar approach of scanning one’s passport to generate a ZK proof.
- [Opacity Labs](http://opacitylabs.com) takes a different angle with Zero-Knowledge Transport Layer Security (zkTLS); their Verified Data Network (VDN) enables a verifiable attestation of any web2 fact (e.g., account ownership or transaction history) that is then portable onchain, without disclosing the underlying data.

Finally, proof-of-personhood takes a different approach. Rather than verifying who someone is, one simply verifies that the wallet is controlled by a unique, living human.

[World ID](https://world.org/world-id) lets users prove they are a unique human without disclosing who they are. It uses a secure hardware device to establish liveness and derive an iris code which is split into cryptographic shares. Independent servers use encrypted multiparty computation to check for a previous enrollment without storing the iris code. Once verified, users can generate zero-knowledge proofs of their verified status without revealing their biometrics or which enrolled person they are.

Sometimes it is sufficient to know someone is a unique human. Additionally, when coupled with identity binding (to prove the identity of the unique human), personhood checks are a powerful tool to combat deepfakes and could help reduce impersonations that become increasingly viable through AI and leaks of KYC databases. World’s Zoom partnership takes this one step further and brings a solution to market that referencing a user’s video feed against their World ID and, if matched, adds a “verified human” badge to their Zoom profile. Another solution is Human Passport, which started as a system for protecting Gitcoin grants. It offers a modular stack for identity verification as well as Sybil defense.

Note that proof of personhood addresses issues like Sybil attacks and deepfakes rather than any regulatory identity requirements and must still be coupled with other KYC approaches to be a complete solution.

These approaches focus on the person behind a wallet. The asset itself raises another set of compliance questions, including where it came from and what restrictions apply to who can hold or transfer it.

### Know Your Asset

Where KYW asks who is holding this asset, KYA asks what this asset is permitted to do, and with whom.

Generally, AML laws paint in broad strokes. The BSA is not concerned with the type of asset involved, which usually only implicates market regulator assessments for appropriate treatment: Is it a security, a commodity, and so on? But KYA can be a very important method for FIs assessing risks across a variety of different compliance rules. KYA points to origin, meaning how the asset was created or originated and who created it, including verification of its compliance characteristics both at issuance and throughout its lifecycle.

The most straightforward implementation is to build transfer restrictions into the token contract at issuance. RWA tokenization platforms such as Securitize embed compliance at the token level. When they issue BlackRock’s BUIDL or Apollo’s ACRED, the token contract itself enforces that transfers can only occur between allowlisted wallets. The asset doesn’t rely on an external gating layer; the token contract enforces specified transfer restrictions. This means the contract rejects transfers that fail its eligibility checks. Ondo’s OUSG and Superstate’s USTB follow a similar pattern: Transfer hooks check an onchain allowlist on every transaction, and both the sender and receiver must be verified before settlement occurs.

The unresolved question in KYA is _provenance_: Verifying not just what a token is, but where it came from. A token issued by a regulated platform with clean KYA has a clear origin story. But as tokens move across bridges, get wrapped, or serve as collateral in DeFi protocols, that provenance trail degrades. Issuance can provide a clear starting record; maintaining and interpreting that record across subsequent activity remains an open problem, and one that connects directly to the Know Your Transaction methods below.

However, this is more of an operational problem rather than a liability trap. The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), the financial intelligence and enforcement agency of the U.S. Department of the Treasury, does not treat an institution as inheriting the sanctions status of every address an asset has passed through. Blockchain analytics distinguish direct exposure (an asset received directly from a designated address) from attenuated, multi-hop exposure. Institutions manage the latter with risk thresholds, quarantine, and suspicious activity reporting, not by refusing assets that have moved through permissionless infrastructure.

### Know Your Transaction

KYT helps institutions assess the risks above by tracking the relationships between different wallets and mapping the flow of an asset across these wallets.

Transaction monitoring is an essential tool financial institutions use to observe customer behaviors and identify suspicious activity that may require reporting. For a specific asset, KYT could include mapping its transaction history across its entire lifecycle, showing which wallets and protocols it has touched. In effect, KYT focuses the scrutiny on the transactions themselves, rather than or in addition to focusing on the person or entity making the transaction. This is particularly useful for meeting ongoing CDD and EDD requirements.

Blockchain analytics, such as Chainalysis, Elliptic, and TRM, among others, can track relationships between different wallets and trace funds through and across blockchains and protocols. Coupled with the use of onchain and offchain data and newly developing AI tools, the technology offered by these firms assists financial institutions in meeting BSA and sanctions compliance obligations for blockchain transactional activity.

Examples of AI tools used for these purposes are Eunice.ai, which tackles risk monitoring and disclosure with their asset classification framework; Didit, which provides screening and transaction monitoring to enable real-time risk analysis on a per-wallet basis; and [Sardine](https://www.sardine.ai/), which performs initial screening as well as daily ongoing transaction monitoring.

In addition to KYW, KYA, and KYT, some blockchains and protocols offer built-in compliance controls. We discuss those below.

## Blockchain-level solutions

Both permissioned and permissionless blockchains increasingly offer more tools to control access and protect privacy. These can block transactions until certain conditions are met and keep sensitive information confidential while allowing regulatory oversight.

The BSA and sanctions laws do not require permissioned validators, identification of every network participant, or access controls across the network. Institutions remain responsible for their own customers and transactions, whichever network they use. They can choose among the designs below based on business and product needs, provided they meet those compliance obligations.

The BSA and sanctions laws do not require permissioned validators, identification of every network participant, or access controls across the network.

For example, on Canton, a Layer one blockchain with configurable privacy, compliance and smart contract logic are deeply interwoven. This is due to its sub-transaction privacy model. Transaction details are only revealed to specific parties with a “need to know.” As another example, Circle’s Arc has a validator model where the validator set is permissioned, but the chain itself is public. Validators are identified participants who have gone through KYC/KYB. On a permissionless network, by contrast, the protocol chooses the validator for each transaction. Processing the transaction does not make that validator a counterparty to the institution or its customer.

Some permissionless protocols also offer features enabling access to permissioned pools or baking in gateways or rules for institutional users to control access. Solana offers a way for RWA issuers to [enforce KYC/AML compliance at the token level](https://github.com/Gitdigital-products/solana-kyc-compliance-sdk?tab=readme-ov-file#readme) through token extensions, specifically “transfer hooks.” Every transfer triggers a check against an onchain allowlist and checks that both the sender and receiver are on the allowlist. If either isn’t verified, the transfer fails at the token level, enforced onchain while the network remains permissionless. The allowlist itself is typically generated in the traditional offchain way.

Uniswap’s v4, a permissionless protocol, has its own “hooks,” which enable custom logic that can be attached to specific points in the swap lifecycle. This allows the creation of permissioned pools. The tokens themselves remain permissionless; it’s the pool that is gated. A gated pool deployed by a third party does not make the protocol permissioned; the party that deploys the pool and sets its access rules is the one that takes on any resulting obligations. Hyperliquid has [begun to test features](https://x.com/HLglobal_/status/2082262395922317619?s=46) allowing HIP-3 deployers to restrict trading to approved addresses only.

Morpho, a decentralized lending platform, lets users and market participants set up their own compliance controls. The protocol itself does not perform KYC or identity verification. In Morpho Blue, its variable rate credit protocol, compliance can be enforced at the asset level when markets use permissioned or whitelisted tokens (such as kycUSDC) as collateral, ensuring that only verified users interact with that specific market.

With Morpho Midnight, an intents-based fixed rate credit protocol, and Morpho Vaults V2, permissioning can be applied with greater flexibility and capital efficiency. Morpho Vaults V2 allows independent curators to implement custom permissioning gates as entry/exit conditions to restrict lender profiles, enabling capital to be allocated to borrowers with specific compliance profiles across the network. This modular design allows institutions that prefer to transact only with verified counterparties to do so through permissioned markets and vaults, while preserving liquidity efficiency across the broader protocol ecosystem. That is a product and risk-appetite choice: an institution’s own compliance obligations do not depend on whether the other participants in a shared market have been verified.

For permissionless markets, providers such as Keyring supply this verification layer without revealing identity. Keyring brings KYC already completed by trusted institutions, such as banks and centralized exchanges, onchain as a zero-knowledge proof, and offers a token wrapper that limits transfers to verified wallets wherever the asset moves.

## Crosschain compliance propagation

Permissioning governs who can participate in a particular market or vault. When assets move between blockchains, issuers and applications face another challenge: Sharing relevant compliance information so they can apply consistent rules across networks.

LayerZero, for example, allows for the crosschain propagation of “compliance state” so that the compliance logic doesn’t have to be rebuilt and maintained separately on each chain. Their Omnichain Fungible Token (OFT) standard supports custom logic hooks, so [issuers can embed KYC/allowlist checks](https://docs.layerzero.network/v2/developers/evm/stablecoin-oft/security-compliance) that must go through on both the source and destination chain before the transfer settles.

LayerZero V2 introduced configurable Decentralized Verifier Networks (DVNs), the entities that validate crosschain messages. A DVN could be configured to enforce compliance checks; for example, whether or not KYC has been performed on a user or wallet owner, screening addresses and other data against sanctions lists, or determining whether Travel Rule metadata is attached before a message is considered valid.

Chainlink also provides a way to link offchain verification with onchain enforcement needs by routing data from various KYC providers onto the blockchain, via [Chainlink’s Automated Compliance Engine](https://chain.link/automated-compliance-engine) (ACE). This also functions as a reusable KYC through the concept of a [CrossChain Identifier (CCID)](https://docs.chain.link/ace), which links a user’s wallets across blockchains: Credentials are verified/attached once and then can be accessed multiple times.

## The bigger picture

These tools address different parts of onchain compliance. Putting them into practice means connecting them with existing compliance programs and finding ways to bring tokenized products to customers.

Partnering with exchanges that have established compliance programs may be the simplest near-term way for institutions to reach more customers. But that is not a compliance requirement. Issuers can also build controls into the tokens themselves, as BUIDL, OUSG, and USDC do in different ways, allowing assets to move on public blockchains subject to those controls.

The next opportunity is to make compliance checks easier to reuse across DeFi. That means enabling an institution or application to assess verified information from another provider against its own requirements. Building this will likely depend on shared protocol standards, compliance-focused software providers, and distribution through incumbents who already hold KYC’ed user bases.

## What’s next? Know Your Agent

Reusable credentials can help establish who a customer is. When an AI agent transacts onchain, manages a vault, or makes payments for a customer, institutions also need to establish who authorized the agent and what it is allowed to do. Know Your Agent extends the discussion to the software acting on a customer’s behalf and the limits of its authority.

Just as humans need credit scores to get loans, agents will need cryptographically signed credentials to transact. This is the emerging Know Your Agent framework: The equivalent of KYC for agents. Without a robust Know Your Agent framework, the answer to the question of who is liable is the untenable and uncomfortable “nobody and everybody.”

Just as humans need credit scores to get loans, agents will need cryptographically signed credentials to transact.

Know Your Agent frameworks require a new kind of credential, one that attests what an agent is authorized to do, on whose behalf, and within what constraints. Each agent must be identifiable and registerable (to a human or business), carry a reputation, and have its constraints validated before it can interact with regulated financial rails. Some solutions work onchain, others offchain, but they increasingly use the same cryptographic primitives, including RFC 9421 signatures and W3C Verifiable Credentials.

![Table comparing Know Your Agent frameworks for AI agent identity, authorization, and payments](https://dwt2zme5yrom6.cloudfront.net/uploads/2026/10/KYA-frameworks-table-selection-1-scaled.png)

### Onchain

ERC-8004, deployed to Ethereum mainnet in January 2026, is one of the first significant blockchain standards for agent identity and attracted more than 30,000 registrations in its first week. It provides a shared onchain system for registering agents, tracking their reputations, and recording independent checks of their work. Each agent has an ERC-721 token minted, which resolves to the agent’s registration file. The onchain history is resistant to tampering and accessible to other applications, reducing dependence on any single platform.

[Self.xyz](http://self.xyz) now has [Self Agent ID](https://docs.self.xyz/docs/agent-id/erc-8004/), which builds on this standard. Self Agent ID, an onchain identity registry, binds AI agent identities to Self human proofs. Each agent has a nontransferable NFT backed by a passport verification, giving applications a reusable way to check that a real person is behind the agent.

Benefits of onchain Know Your Agent approaches include immutability and credible neutrality, as well as composability.

### Offchain

Many approaches use offchain credentials and signed messages to identify agents and define their permissions, even when payments happen onchain. The examples below address different parts of agent activity, including proving authorization, enforcing spending limits, and protecting the keys used to sign transactions:

- **Google’s Agent Payments Protocol (AP2)** uses signed [“mandates”](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/announcing-agents-to-payments-ap2-protocol) to record a user’s instructions, including spending limits and purchase conditions. These provide verifiable evidence of what an agent is authorized to do.
- **Catena Labs’ Agent Commerce Kit** provides tools for agent identity, authorization, and payments. Its proposed [ACK v2](https://catena.com/blog/ack-v2-smaller-identity-core-x402-payment-profile) uses signed grants that specify who authorized an agent and what it can do. Each request includes the grant and a standard HTTP message signature, defined in RFC 9421.
- **Skyfire’s KYAPay** lets agents identify themselves, show who they represent, and make payments using signed digital credentials called JSON Web Tokens (JWTs). Skyfire also works with Experian’s Agent Trust framework to connect agents with verified consumers and devices.
- **Circle’s Agent Wallets** focus on custody and spending controls. Signing-key shares remain hidden from the agent, while users retain custody. Agents can transact autonomously within spending limits and recipient restrictions set by the user.
- **Anchorage Agentic Banking** gives each agent credentials tied to a specific user and organization, with permission to spend from designated budgets. Transactions are logged under the agent’s identity, and its access can be revoked.
- **Mastercard’s Agent Pay** registers agents and connects their payments to consumer consent and tokenized payment credentials. Its partnership with Cloudflare uses signed web requests to help merchants authenticate agents visiting their sites.
- **Visa’s Intelligent Commerce** replaces card details with digital payment tokens that confirm an agent has permission to act for a consumer. Consumers set spending limits and conditions for purchases.
- **Zero Hash’s Agentic Finance Suite** screens agents and the people or businesses behind them before allowing transactions. It also lets users delegate permissions and control what each agent can do.
- **Ledger** is building tools that connect agents to secure hardware and the humans who authorize them. Its roadmap combines agent identity, hardware-enforced spending rules, and human approval for sensitive actions.

Delegating financial activity to agents adds questions about authorization and control, bringing the discussion back to how institutions apply compliance checks within the products and services they provide.

Bringing finance onchain is a chance to improve how compliance works. None of the approaches above require new legislation — Treasury’s rules already allow non-documentary verification, the September 2026 FAQs recognize verifiable digital credentials within CIP, and FinCEN has said institutions will not face enforcement solely for responsibly experimenting with new technology. Institutions that want to avoid redundant KYC, rather than KYC itself, can start with the tools available today.

content_html:
Python 3.15 is here! Here's the essential What's new in Python 3.15 guide, this year curated by 3.14 and 3.15 release manager Hugo van Kemenade. As someone who builds open source software that works in every supported Python version, I get to say goodbye to Python 3.10 and start embracing features from Python 3.11.

First, some highlights from Python 3.15.

Explicit lazy imports

I'm most excited about Explicit lazy imports from PEP 810. These let you import modules like so:

lazy import json
lazy from pathlib import Path

The module will then be imported the first time those symbols are used in the code that follows.

My LLM CLI tool implements plugins. I had to recommend manual lazy imports in the plugin author documentation, because simply installing plugins that used heavy dependencies such as sentence_transformers could add multiple seconds to every invocation of the llm command. Lazy imports directly address this startup cost.

Unpacking in comprehensions

The new [*sublist for sublist in lists] unpacking syntax is neat. Here's an illustration lifted from the documentation:

lists = [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5]]
[*L for L in lists]
# [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
# equivalent to [x for L in lists for x in L]

sets = [{1, 2}, {2, 3}, {3, 4}]
{*s for s in sets}
# {1, 2, 3, 4}
# equivalent to {x for s in sets for x in s}

dicts = [{'a': 1}, {'b': 2}, {'a': 3}]
{**d for d in dicts}
# {'a': 3, 'b': 2}
# equivalent to {k: v for d in dicts for k,v in d.items()}

PEP 798: Unpacking in Comprehensions by Adam Hartz and Erik Demaine proposed this as an extension of the unpacking syntax from PEP 448, which landed in Python 3.5 back in 2015.

A sampling profiler

Python's existing tracing profiler has been renamed from cProfile to profiling.tracing, and has been joined by an exciting new sampling profiler called Tachyon, aka profiling.sampling.

Sampling profilers work by periodically capturing stack traces from running processes, then using those to calculate which functions have the most time spent inside of them. They're very low overhead and can provide a deep insight into running systems, without needing to instrument those systems first.

I've previously used tools like py-spy for this. Now this capability is baked into the standard library.

If you have the PID of an existing Python 3.15 process you can start gathering samples by running this (I had to use sudo on macOS):

sudo uv run --python 3.15 python -m profiling.sampling attach 1234

Interact with the main program a bit, then hit Ctrl+C to stop gathering and see a report, which looks something like this:

It can also produce flame graphs like this and heat maps like this, and can even output a format that can be viewed in the Firefox profiler UI.

3.15 isn't much faster than 3.14

Miguel Grinberg investigated How fast is Python 3.15? the other day against the 3.15.0rc3 release and found performance to be mostly the same as 3.14, with the exception of the experimental JIT. The JIT gave a 1.2x boost over the standard 3.15 interpreter (on a Fibonacci test), the first time Miguel observed a meaningful JIT performance increase.

Miguel's explorations of 3.14 last year found significant boosts against Python 3.13 across many more categories.

Upgrading to Python 3.15 with uv

I used the following sequence of commands to get uv to use Python 3.15 on my Mac. First I had to upgrade uv itself to ensure it knew about the new release:

uv self update

Then I installed the stable 3.15 release:

uv python install 3.15

And told uv that I wanted that to be the default for every uv run command, unless the project itself pinned a different version:

uv python pin --global 3.15

Now the following reports 3.15 as the version:

uv run python --version

I already have a bunch of tools installed using uv tool install. I reinstalled them to use Python 3.15 like this:

uv tool upgrade datasette --python 3.15

Then I can confirm the version like this:

datasette --get /-/versions.json | jq

Highlights from Python 3.11

The release of 3.15 means that Python 3.10 (released in 2021) is officially no longer supported.

My policy for my main open source projects is to keep them working in every supported Python version. I can now drop 3.10 and start using features that were introduced in 3.11.

Here's the What's new in Python 3.11 document. I finally get to rely on tomllib being available!

Datasette makes extensive use of asyncio. 3.11 adds TaskGroup and timeout(), and several more new features.

datetime.UTC is a new in 3.11 alias for datetime.timezone.utc.

Python's SQLite support got some significant upgrades in 3.11, including:

  • setlimit() and getlimit() expose a mechanism for setting SQLite runtime limits from Python.
  • create_window_function() lets us create custom window functions in Python, as a class with step(), value(), inverse(), and finalize() methods.
  • blobopen() provides an efficient mechanism for partial reads and writes of large BLOB binary values stored in a SQLite row.
  • You can now call set_authorizer(None) to remove a SQLite authorizer. Datasette had a workaround for this!

Plus a whole bunch of improvements to Python's typing system.

I plan to land Python 3.11 improvements to a bunch of my projects over the next few weeks. Here's my first Datasette PR removing that set_authorizer(None) workaround.

I've also updated my click-app, datasette-plugin, python-lib, and llm-plugin cookiecutter templates to test against Python 3.11 through Python 3.15.

#### Explicit lazy imports


The new `[*sublist for sublist in lists]` unpacking syntax is neat. Here's an illustration [lifted from the documentation](https://docs.python.org/3.15/whatsnew/3.15.html#pep-798-unpacking-in-comprehensions):

```
lists = [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5]]
[*L for L in lists]
# [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
# equivalent to [x for L in lists for x in L]

sets = [{1, 2}, {2, 3}, {3, 4}]
{*s for s in sets}
# {1, 2, 3, 4}
# equivalent to {x for s in sets for x in s}

dicts = [{'a': 1}, {'b': 2}, {'a': 3}]
{**d for d in dicts}
# {'a': 3, 'b': 2}
# equivalent to {k: v for d in dicts for k,v in d.items()}
```

[PEP 798: Unpacking in Comprehensions](https://peps.python.org/pep-0798/) by Adam Hartz and Erik Demaine proposed this as an extension of the unpacking syntax [from PEP 448](https://peps.python.org/pep-0448/), which landed [in Python 3.5](https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.5.html#pep-448-additional-unpacking-generalizations) back in 2015.

#### A sampling profiler

Python's existing tracing profiler has been renamed from `cProfile` to [profiling.tracing](https://docs.python.org/3.15/library/profiling.tracing.html#module-profiling.tracing), and has been joined by an exciting new sampling profiler called Tachyon, aka [profiling.sampling](https://docs.python.org/3.15/whatsnew/3.15.html#tachyon-high-frequency-statistical-sampling-profiler).

Sampling profilers work by periodically capturing stack traces from running processes, then using those to calculate which functions have the most time spent inside of them. They're very low overhead and can provide a deep insight into running systems, without needing to instrument those systems first.

I've [previously used tools](https://simonwillison.net/tags/profiling/) like [py-spy](https://github.com/benfred/py-spy) for this. Now this capability is baked into the standard library.

If you have the PID of an existing Python 3.15 process you can start gathering samples by running this (I had to use `sudo` on macOS):

```
sudo uv run --python 3.15 python -m profiling.sampling attach 1234
```

Interact with the main program a bit, then hit Ctrl+C to stop gathering and see a report, which looks something like this:

![Screenshot of terminal output from a Python sampling profiler with colored text on a black background. Header lines report 2,651 samples captured in 2.65 seconds at a sample rate of 999.98 samples/sec with an error rate of 0.19. A Profile Stats table with columns for nsamples, sample%, tottime, cumul%, cumtime and filename:lineno(function) shows that 99.9% of samples (2.644 seconds) were spent directly in selectors.py KqueueSelector.select, meaning the process was almost entirely idle waiting on the asyncio event loop. The rest of the table lists the call stack beneath it with zero direct time but 100% cumulative presence: asyncio base_events.py run_once, run_forever and run_until_complete, runners.py Runner.run and run, cli.py serve and sqlite_extensions wrapped, and several click core.py invoke, main and call frames. A legend explains each column, followed by a Summary of Interesting Functions section listing hot spots (KqueueSelector.select at 99.9% direct samples), the most frequently present functions on the stack (run_forever, run_until_complete and Runner.run at 100%), and the highest call magnification (2645.0x for BaseEventLoop._run_once).](https://static.simonwillison.net/static/2026/profiler-output.webp)

It can also produce [flame graphs like this](https://simonw.github.io/research/python-3-15-web-edit-profiling/artifacts/flamegraph.html) and [heat maps like this](https://simonw.github.io/research/python-3-15-web-edit-profiling/artifacts/heatmap/index.html), and can even output a format that can be viewed in the Firefox profiler UI.

#### 3.15 isn't much faster than 3.14

Miguel Grinberg investigated [How fast is Python 3.15?](https://blog.miguelgrinberg.com/post/how-fast-is-python-3-15) the other day against the 3.15.0rc3 release and found performance to be mostly the same as 3.14, with the exception of the experimental JIT. The JIT gave a 1.2x boost over the standard 3.15 interpreter (on a Fibonacci test), the first time Miguel observed a meaningful JIT performance increase.

Miguel's [explorations of 3.14](https://blog.miguelgrinberg.com/post/python-3-14-is-here-how-fast-is-it) last year found significant boosts against Python 3.13 across many more categories.

#### Upgrading to Python 3.15 with uv

I used the following sequence of commands to get `uv` to use Python 3.15 on my Mac. First I had to upgrade `uv` itself to ensure it knew about the new release:

```
uv self update
```

Then I installed the stable 3.15 release:

```
uv python install 3.15
```

And told `uv` that I wanted that to be the default for every `uv run` command, unless the project itself pinned a different version:

```
uv python pin --global 3.15
```

Now the following reports 3.15 as the version:

```
uv run python --version
```

I already have a bunch of tools installed using `uv tool install`. I reinstalled them to use Python 3.15 like this:

```
uv tool upgrade datasette --python 3.15
```

Then I can confirm the version like this:

```
datasette --get /-/versions.json | jq
```

#### Highlights from Python 3.11

The release of 3.15 means that Python 3.10 (released in 2021) is officially [no longer supported](https://devguide.python.org/versions/).

My policy for my main open source projects is to keep them working in every supported Python version. I can now drop 3.10 and start using features that were introduced in 3.11.

Here's the [What's new in Python 3.11](https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.11.html) document. I finally get to rely on [tomllib](https://docs.python.org/3/library/tomllib.html#module-tomllib) being available!

Datasette makes extensive use of `asyncio`. 3.11 adds [TaskGroup](https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-task.html#asyncio.TaskGroup) and [timeout()](https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio-task.html#asyncio.timeout), and [several more](https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.11.html#asyncio) new features.

`datetime.UTC` is a new in 3.11 alias for `datetime.timezone.utc`.

Python's SQLite support got some significant upgrades in 3.11, including:

- [setlimit()](https://docs.python.org/3/library/sqlite3.html#sqlite3.Connection.setlimit) and [getlimit()](https://docs.python.org/3/library/sqlite3.html#sqlite3.Connection.getlimit) expose a mechanism for setting [SQLite runtime limits](https://www.sqlite.org/c3ref/c_limit_attached.html) from Python.
- [create\_window\_function()](https://docs.python.org/3/library/sqlite3.html#sqlite3.Connection.create_window_function) lets us create custom window functions in Python, as a class with `step()`, `value()`, `inverse()`, and `finalize()` methods.
- [blobopen()](https://docs.python.org/3/library/sqlite3.html#sqlite3.Connection.blobopen) provides an efficient mechanism for partial reads and writes of large `BLOB` binary values stored in a SQLite row.
- You can now call `set_authorizer(None)` to remove a SQLite authorizer. Datasette had a workaround for this!

Plus a whole bunch of [improvements to Python's typing system](https://docs.python.org/3/whatsnew/3.11.html#new-feat-related-type-hints-311).

I plan to land Python 3.11 improvements to a bunch of my projects over the next few weeks. Here's [my first Datasette PR](https://github.com/simonw/datasette/pull/2998) removing that `set_authorizer(None)` workaround.

I've also updated my [click-app](https://github.com/simonw/click-app), [datasette-plugin](https://github.com/simonw/datasette-plugin), [python-lib](https://github.com/simonw/python-lib), and [llm-plugin](https://github.com/simonw/llm-plugin) cookiecutter templates to test against Python 3.11 through Python 3.15.

title: Dwarf Fortress uses version control now
summary: I remember hearing a while ago that Dwarf Fortress didn't use version control. That fact has been lodged in my head, because given its inherent complexity I have trouble imagining a codebase that would benefit from version control _more_. That's art. I went looking and I'm sad t...
content_html:
I remember hearing a while ago that Dwarf Fortress didn't use version control. That fact has been lodged in my head, because given its inherent complexity I have trouble imagining a codebase that would benefit from version control more. That's art.

I went looking and I'm sad to report that the days without version control appear to have ended. Quoting Tarn Adams over time:

  • March 2013: "I don't use version control -- I didn't like the feeling of having the code get committed into a black box thingy with no immediate upside"
  • March 2016: "I don’t even use version control. If you don’t know what that is then you’re not gonna yell at me. If you even know what version control is you’re gonna be like, ‘You don’t use version control? You don’t use source control? What is wrong with you? How can you even work? I’m just not cut out for it, in a sense. It’s been 15 years, so the reasons have change over time, but that’s my current understanding of it." 
  • March 2023: "I've got Discord channels to check and version control stuff to use now, so the process is definitely a little more involved"

That March 2023 quote comes from an interview about the release on Steam which made them millionaires. I'm a tiny bit sad that they gave in before they hit that milestone, but what an impressive run.

title: Deno is joining Cloudflare
summary: **[Deno is joining Cloudflare](https://deno.com/blog/cloudflare)** The Deno team released the first version of [celld](https://github.com/denoland/celld) back in August - their open source implementation of the Durable Objects pattern from Cloudflare Workers. Today, Cloudflare a...
content_html:
Deno is joining Cloudflare

The Deno team released the first version of celld back in August - their open source implementation of the Durable Objects pattern from Cloudflare Workers.

Today, Cloudflare are acquiring Deno outright, with the goal of building on celld to "make workerd self-hosting a first-class supported way to build and run apps using the Workers programming model" (see the Cloudflare blog.)

The bad news is that Deno itself will not be maintained by Cloudflare beyond the next year:

We will support the Deno runtime for another year with monthly releases containing bug fixes and security updates. After that year we will end our development of the Deno runtime. Deno will remain open source, and we welcome others who want to continue its development.

Deno (and Node.js) creator Ryan Dahl explained that decision in a comment on Hacker News:

It's a joint decision and I agree with it. I'm most invested in its success and have put the most work into it - and I no longer think it's where I can do the most important work. There are some good ideas in Deno and it's well engineered - but it ultimately is not solving big problems. It has been sucked into the gravity well of node compatibility, which forces it to behave exactly as Node does. Why reimplement Node? It works. Marginal performance or UX or security benefits are not enough.

I'm interested in building powerful new abstractions. celld has been working remarkably well, depending only on object storage for coordination and persistence. It is not just a slightly different API to interact with the file system or network - it's an entirely new model for server development.

My favorite feature of Deno has long been the permissions system, where you can run a Deno script and specify exactly which files and folders it can read and write to, and which network hosts it can access.

Node.js has a similar permissions model these days, added in Node v20.0.0 in April 2023 and declared stable in Node v22.13.0 in January 2025. They don't yet support allow-listing specific network hosts though - networking is either on or off.

Via Hacker News

title: Can AI Actually Break Cryptography? Experts Weigh In On the FUD

content_html:
with Dan Boneh, Eddy Lazzarin, Justin Thaler and Liz Harkavy

AI is getting better at solving hard math problems. But what does that mean for the cryptography protecting everything from banking and private messages to crypto wallets and more?

We bring together expert cryptographers from Stanford and a16z crypto to make sense of the recent warnings sounded on social media, partly sparked by OpenAI’s drop of recent math results. We cover what’s fact, what’s assumption; what’s new and which risks cryptographers have long prepared for; where quantum computing fits; and where they see opportunities for builders to make software more secure.

Highlights:

00:00 Intro
00:37 What sparked the debate about AI and cryptography
01:35 Signal vs. noise: What the math does and doesn’t tell us
05:29 Why cryptography depends on open problems
09:25 Why the stakes go beyond blockchains
10:43 How AI could strengthen confidence in cryptography
13:50 Considerations for users and institutions
20:10 Where AI and quantum threats overlap
22:32 Building systems that can change cryptographic methods
23:59 Hash-based versus lattice-based cryptography
33:07 Opportunities for builders and better security tools

content_html:
I shipped a new feature for my blog today: the Newsletters page, which offers an index of all of the newsletters I've sent out, both my free weekly Substack and my monthly sponsors-only updates. I built the feature almost entirely using my voice, chatting away to my laptop while I cooked dinner.

Codex voice mode

I used the ChatGPT desktop app for this, in the Codex tab, using the voice conversation mode, running against a local development environment. Here's what that looks like:

I started the session against my local simonwillisonblog checkout by typing:

Start dev server and open in browser

This gave me a preview of the site that it would be working on, and meant that I could later ask it to show me the new pages so I could visually track its progress.

Then I clicked the "Start new voice chat" button - that's not the microphone button, it's the one to the right of it - and set my laptop up in the kitchen so I could talk to it while I cooked.

Talking to my computer

I had a pretty good idea of what I wanted to build, and it's a simple enough Django feature that I was certain the model (in this case GPT-6 Astra High) would be able to do it. A new model, a migration, some view code, templates, and a couple of import functions to populate the database from external sources.

Here's an extract of my voice transcript that was captured by Codex:

Um, they do not. Um, this is going to be a new type of content. Um, it's not going to show up... Oh, hold on. Yeah, no- I do not want this to show up in my, um, tag pages and date archive pages and... Actually, no, I think... I don't want it on the tag pages. I don't want it on the, um, blog index page. But I think I do want it to show up on the date-based pages. You know, if you navigate to September the 19th, and I sent a newsletter on that page, I think I want that to show up. So... this is- so I think we probably need a new model. The other thing is that I want them searchable, uh the Substack ones are not searchable, because those are actually just copies of other s- on content on my blog. These monthly ones do contain unique content, and spe- and once they're... published, like once they're made public a month after they've gone out, I want them to show up on my search results.

Apparently this was clear enough that the model knew what I wanted to build! You can read the full transcript, disfluencies and all, in this Gist.

We went on like this for about half an hour (the time it took to cook dinner). The model would reply and occasionally ask clarifying questions, then get to work modifying the code.

What we built

We got a surprisingly long way entirely by voice:

  • A new model and migration to represent imported newsletters in Django, plus Django Admin configuration for that
  • Four working imports:
    • The most recent Substack items via RSS
    • Every other Substack item via their undocumented API, which GPT-6 Astra knew about (it tried /api/v1/archive directly) and then ran a search to figure out how to paginate it and found this article by Karen Spinner
    • All of my published monthly newsletters from my simonw/monthly-newsletter-archive GitHub repository
    • My most recent private sponsors-only newsletter from a private repository
  • The /newsletters/ and /newsletters/2026/ public archive pages
  • Newsletters showing up on day and month archive pages too, but not on tag pages or my homepage
  • Weekly Substack newsletters link to Substack; archived monthly newsletters have their own pages
  • Integration with my site search engine

It was almost ready to ship. The catch was the imports: Astra offered to export data from my local copy so I could import that into production, but I wanted it to work like my other import scripts. Since some of the data lived in a private GitHub repository, this would involve creating a new API key, and for that I knew I'd have to sit at the keyboard for a while.

Finishing it with a review

Once I had finished cooking and judged it mostly feature-complete, I had Codex create a branch and open a pull request.

I reviewed the code in the GitHub PR interface. It was nearly what I needed, except it had chosen to use Git in a subprocess for one of the import scripts. I needed one of the imports to pull from a private Git repository, so I figured the API would be a better bet. I switched to typing and had Codex swap that out for an API-based import instead.

You can see the changes I made during the review in the extra commits on the PR. I fixed the import mechanism and made a few tweaks to the display of those public pages. It took an additional half hour of typing-based prompting to get to the point where I was happy to deploy it to production by landing the PR.

The end result

You can see the end result at the new newsletters index page, or view the page for a previous monthly newsletter.

The index page shows my most recent Substack weekly newsletters and GitHub sponsors monthly newsletters mixed together in reverse chronological order. Further down the page are links to my by-year archive pages.

GPT-6 Astra designed the page, and then tweaked that design based on my vocal feedback from glancing at the local preview across the kitchen.

Better for multi-tasking than as a daily driver

OpenAI love using voice-driven demos like this one for things like DevDay - and they do work well in that environment. I don't think this is going to be a daily driver for me though.

I've written before about how much "work" I get done using ChatGPT voice mode on my phone while walking the dog - mostly research and brainstorming, but occasionally actual development work by having ChatGPT write and test out snippets of code.

This feels different. The addition of the visual preview, plus being able to type or paste things in via the keyboard when I need to communicate something that doesn't work vocally, makes this a much more powerful way of interacting with a coding agent.

I still switch back to typing once I get down to the details of things though. Being able to paste in examples and error messages, or directly highlight the code or feature that needs changing, remains more efficient than trying to describe it in words.

I mainly work from home, which is good because there's no way I'd want to talk to my computer like this in a shared workspace!

The killer feature for me is the ability to multi-task. I usually cook with a podcast or TikTok running; now I can actually build stuff instead.

content_html:
Release: ttok 1.0

I released ttok 0.4, ran uv tool upgrade ttok, piped a file into the new version... and realized that it was defaulting to the GPT-4 tokenizer when it should very clearly default to GPT-5/GPT-6 instead!

I figured switching the default was a reasonable excuse to finally ship a 1.0.

OpenAI haven't actually confirmed that GPT-6 uses the same tokenizer as the GPT-5 family yet - there's an angry issue about it - but I found this commit by William Liu which reports on an experiment he ran confirming that the tokenizers are likely the same:

All seven GPT models (5.5, 5.6 Sol/Terra/Luna, 6 Astra/Sol/Luna) report 44,794 tokens and match each other on every one of the 31 fixtures. GPT-6 introduces no input-count change on this corpus.

I've always been kind of into computers since I was young. And then when film started to move from analog film to digital, I became more interested in that aspect of it. And the visual effects workflow for many years has included machine learning.

So I can write like pretty shitty Python scripts and stuff like that because with convolutional neural networks, which were the sort of precursors to what the transformer can do, which is just much more computation simultaneously, you would do things like look at what's called a tensor, which is just the numerical translation of a visual image in numbers — like the batch number, the frame number, the red, green, and blue values of each pixel in each frame.

And a tensor, you use a convolutional neural network to identify patterns in that that would reveal what's called edge detection or feature extraction, which is just identifying patterns enough to know like this is where the window ledge is, so we can more easily take the green screen image out and replace it with something.

The previous Haiku, 4.5, was very much showing its age. It came out almost a year ago, and was priced at $1/million input and $5/million output - relatively expensive even back then, and a full 10x the price of OpenAI's GPT-6 Luna, released last month.

The new Haiku exactly matches the price of GPT-6 Luna - $0.10/$0.50 - up to 100,000 tokens. Beyond 100,000 tokens the price increases 5x to $0.50/$2.50. Luna itself has a price increase at 272,000 tokens but only to $0.20/$0.75.

Haiku 5.5 also uses a new, less generous tokenizer. My Claude Token Counter tool shows that the same long prompt uses around 1.25x as many tokens with Haiku 5.5 compared to Haiku 4.5, so there's a hidden price increase there.

If your workloads fit in 100,000 tokens, Haiku is the same price as Luna and reports higher benchmark scores. Above 100,000 tokens, Luna looks like a much better deal.

The most recent release of llm-anthropic finally fixed it so I don't need to ship a new version of that plugin for every new model. I tested the new model like this:

llm install -U llm-anthropic
llm anthropic refresh
llm -m claude-haiku-5.5 "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" -o thinking_effort low

Pelicans

Here are pelicans for low, medium, high, xhigh, and max. The new Haiku doesn't let you disable reasoning, and defaults to medium. I got a good bicycle frame for everything beyond low. The low effort pelican cost 0.0936 cents and took 7 seconds.

This max effort pelican (with a reasoning trace that starts "This is the classic pelican-on-bicycle SVG test...") took 5 minutes 9 seconds to generate, but still only cost me 3.3826 cents:

And a generous API credit scheme for subscribers

In addition to Haiku 5.5, Anthropic announced today that they are halving the price of cache reads for Sonnet 5.5. They've also added API credits to subscription plans:

Second, this week, we’ll roll out a new monthly API credit to all Max and Team subscribers for use on the Claude Platform. Max 5x users will get $100 in credits per month, Max 20x users will get $200, and Team subscribers will receive up to $500, pooled across their users.

Claiming this is pleasantly easy: navigate to Settings -> Billing and select the API organization that should benefit from the credits every month:

content_html:
Anti-Patterns in Software Blogging

Some excellent writing advice from Michael Lynch. Michael warns against "meandering intros", misjudging your reader's existing knowledge, assuming they'll read your previous posts, and excessive formality.

He also warns against overreliance on links as an excuse not to explain terminology. This one hurt! I do this all the time, but I have a nagging suspicion that almost nobody ever clicks on them.

(In a Lobste.rs comment Michael clarifies that "My rule of thumb is that my article should still make sense to the reader even if they don't click any links". That works for me.)

This point about using your own voice is crucial:

Beginner software bloggers suffer from a mass delusion that you have to write in a stiff, overly formal way for people to take you seriously [...]

Just write the way you talk.

With so many developers delegating their writing to AI, software blogging is becoming bland and homogenous. Readers are hungry for writing with personality.

Via Lobste.rs

content_html:
OpenAI “rogue” agent activities found on Wikimedia projects

Given how tempting a target wikis are for rogue agent swarms, it's not a huge surprise that Wikipedia found evidence of that activity once they went looking:

The Wikimedia Foundation conducted its own investigation to see whether Wikimedia websites had been similarly affected by AI agents, focusing on those operated by OpenAI. We can confirm that we have discovered some activity by these “rogue” OpenAI agents on Wikimedia platforms. The unauthorized bot activities included edits to our wikis, some unsuccessful attempts to exploit a public note-taking tool we host, and heavy traffic, which are described more below.

They found evidence of agents editing sandbox pages, trying to use pieces of infrastructure such as Etherpad to help proxy content from elsewhere, and saw widespread crawling and "hundreds of thousands of data queries" to their Wikidata Query Service.

My best guess is that most of this was a similar (or the same) swarm of agents as those that defaced that German wiki while training for research tasks.

The Wikipedia sandbox wiki edits appear to have started on May 12th, and the initial test edits to the UseModWiki Sandbox page reported by that incident started on May 11th.
